messages.subject: Item information matrix
parts:
Hello, 
I have several questions concerning the item information matrix and selection criteria used in mirt and mirtCAT. These could be elementary questions for somebody here, but I am - as a non-statistician - struggling :-) All the questions are related to a confirmatory multidimensional model with correlated traits, where each item has only one or two non-zero loadings.

First of all, I have a problem conceptually understanding what do the off-diagonal elements of the item information matrix (IIM) represent. Is it un uncertainty related to the difference (or trade-off) between two thetas estimates?

Second, I want to estimate information in the direction of the single dimension. Therefore, the angle between this single direction and my dimension is zero. Thus the weight of a particular element in IIM will be 1 (as the cos(0) = 1 = r). But what about the other dimensions? Will these weights be zero, or should I add the factor correlation? An example: I have two traits correlated r = 0.5. An item has the two factor loadings a_1 = 0.6 and a_2 = 0.7. The item information matrix would be


If I consider the angle 0 and 90 (r = {r_1 = 1, r_2 = 0}), the weighted IIM would be

However, the traits are correlated, r = .5. Therefore, the question is whether angles 0 and 90 degrees are admissible. Shouldn't I use angles r = {r_1 = 1, r_2 = .5}, where the second angle represents the correlation of both traits? In such a case, IIM would be equal to


The latter gives me a sense as off-diagonals are related to discriminations between traits, and therefore, they are not zero. With highly correlated traits, off-diagonals elements will be close to zero, representing the inability to discriminate between correlated dimensions, and vice versa. However, an item could add information even in the factor with zero loading in the latter. Is it correct?

The other question is related to item selection criteria. I did not find any documentation of them, so I ask here:
  1. D-rule (IIM determinant) - this maximalize the ability to estimate each trait and discriminate between them, as it uses the whole information matrix?
  2. T-rule (IIm diagonal) - this maximalize only the ability to estimate each trait, as it does not consider the off-diagonal elements?
  3. A-rule (covariance matrix diagonal) - similar to T-rule, but work with an error matrix (inversed item information matrix)?
  4. E-rule: I do not understand here. In mirt help, it is written: "the minimum value of the information matrix". Why does anybody want to use that?
  5. W-rule: the same here. What means "the weighted information criteria"? Shouldn't be here a "weighted information matrix"?

Finally, for D-rule, T-rule, and E-rule, it is written "potentially weighted matrix". The matrix is therefore weighted using factors correlation matrix, right?

Thank you for the answer; I am really stuck.

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Item information matrix
parts: Hi Hynek,

On Tue, Mar 22, 2022 at 9:04 AM Hynek Cígler <cigler...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hello, 
I have several questions concerning the item information matrix and selection criteria used in mirt and mirtCAT. These could be elementary questions for somebody here, but I am - as a non-statistician - struggling :-) All the questions are related to a confirmatory multidimensional model with correlated traits, where each item has only one or two non-zero loadings.

First of all, I have a problem conceptually understanding what do the off-diagonal elements of the item information matrix (IIM) represent. Is it un uncertainty related to the difference (or trade-off) between two thetas estimates?

The off-diagonal elements have to do with whether the item correlates with both traits (i.e., has non-zero slopes for each), in which case the item will measures something about more than one variable (diagonal terms) with some degree of shared information (off-diagonal). Items containing only one unique loading will have zers everywhere except their respective diagonal.

Second, I want to estimate information in the direction of the single dimension. Therefore, the angle between this single direction and my dimension is zero. Thus the weight of a particular element in IIM will be 1 (as the cos(0) = 1 = r). But what about the other dimensions? Will these weights be zero, or should I add the factor correlation?

You would want set the weights of the other dimensions to zero, though rarely is this something that I recommend doing (unless you are searching for some maximal multidimensional information location, in which case MDIFF is the answer).

An example: I have two traits correlated r = 0.5. An item has the two factor loadings a_1 = 0.6 and a_2 = 0.7. The item information matrix would be


If I consider the angle 0 and 90 (r = {r_1 = 1, r_2 = 0}), the weighted IIM would be

However, the traits are correlated, r = .5. Therefore, the question is whether angles 0 and 90 degrees are admissible. Shouldn't I use angles r = {r_1 = 1, r_2 = .5}, where the second angle represents the correlation of both traits? In such a case, IIM would be equal to


The latter gives me a sense as off-diagonals are related to discriminations between traits, and therefore, they are not zero. With highly correlated traits, off-diagonals elements will be close to zero, representing the inability to discriminate between correlated dimensions, and vice versa. However, an item could add information even in the factor with zero loading in the latter. Is it correct?
This sounds correct from what I gather you're trying to do. Unidimensional items still provide information about other latent traits if indeed the traits are modeled to be correlated.
The other question is related to item selection criteria. I did not find any documentation of them, so I ask here:
Did you refer to the associated JSS article?
1. D-rule (IIM determinant) - this maximalize the ability to estimate each trait and discriminate between them, as it uses the whole information matrix?
Yes, and analogously minimizes the expected measurement error by way of the determinant geometry.
1. T-rule (IIm diagonal) - this maximalize only the ability to estimate each trait, as it does not consider the off-diagonal elements?
Correct.
1. A-rule (covariance matrix diagonal) - similar to T-rule, but work with an error matrix (inversed item information matrix)?
Yes, and can behave differently (arguably, more optimally) when user-defined weights are included.
1. E-rule: I do not understand here. In mirt help, it is written: "the minimum value of the information matrix". Why does anybody want to use that?
You generally don't, unless you're looking to uniformly minimize the general variance of the trait estimates.
1. W-rule: the same here. What means "the weighted information criteria"? Shouldn't be here a "weighted information matrix"?
Is there a difference? Weights are applied to the information matrix to result in a scalar.
Finally, for D-rule, T-rule, and E-rule, it is written "potentially weighted matrix". The matrix is therefore weighted using factors correlation matrix, right?

Not quite, these are based on user-defined weights, where you may be working with a multidimensional test but really only want to select items that pertain to a specific dimension (such as the general factor in a bi-factor model). HTH.

Phil
Thank you for the answer; I am really stuck.

messages.author: 498625331dc5ad8c
messages.subject: Re: Item information matrix
parts:
Dear Phil,
Thank you for the detailed response again; I hate my spam folder!
I solved the problem successfully; we soon realized that in a multidimensional setting, an information matrix cannot be used to estimate measurement errors. Unfortunately, estimating the Hessian matrix in Python with acceptable numerical stability was terrible. Thank you for having mirt as a benchmark!
